Senator Anne Carney, Senate Chair Representative Amy Kuhn, House Chair Committee on Judiciary 100 State House Station, Room 438 Augusta, Maine 04333-0100
Re: LD 1008, An Act to Require the Attorney General to Seek Legislative Approval Before Filing Any Civil Suit on Behalf of the State and to Authorize Citizen-initiated Petitions to Move for Dismissal
Dear Senator Carney and Representative Kuhn:
I am writing in opposition to L.D. 1008, An Act to Require the Attorney General to Seek Legislative Approval Before Filing Any Civil Suit on Behalf of the State and to Authorize Citizeninitiated Petitions to Move for Dismissal.
This bill would prohibit the Attorney General from filing any civil lawsuit on behalf of the State unless the Legislature passes, and the Governor signs, legislation expressly authorizing the action. And even when the Attorney General has been so authorized, any registered voter may submit to the Secretary of State an application to initiate a petition directing the Attorney General to dismiss the lawsuit. Upon the submission of an application by a single voter the Attorney General must stay the litigation while the petition is circulated. If, within a year, 500 people sign the petition, the Attorney General must dismiss the lawsuit.
This bill would likely violate separation of powers principles and would substantially interfere with the work of the office. First, Maine's Law Court has recognized that while some of the Attorney General's duties are defined by statute, the Attorney General is a constitutional officer and has independent common law duties, the most important of which is to "protect the interest of the general public." Superintendent of Insurance v. Attorney General, 558 A.2d 1197 (Me. 1989). Moreover, the Attorney General is not part of the legislative, executive or judicial branches of government. Opinion of the Justices, 2015 ME 27, � 8. In order for the Attorney General to properly carry out their duties, it is critical that no other branch of government unduly interfere with the Attorney General's ability to take such actions as determined necessary to protect the public interest.

Senator Anne Carney, Senate Chair Representative Amy Kuhn, House Chair March ___, 2025 Page 2
Second, even if this bill did not violate separation of powers principles, it would cripple the Attorney General's ability to use one of the most important tools for protecting the public interest: the initiation of litigation. The Attorney General often must use lawsuits to collect money owed the State, protect the public from incompetent licensed professionals, enforce Maine's consumer protections laws, and mitigate the effects of, and recover damages for, environmental and other harms inflicted on our State. By subjecting the initiation of litigation to the legislative process, this bill would, at the very least, result in significant delays before the Attorney General could act. It also raises concerns about how the public legislative process could be used to debate the merits of initiating litigation, given that the underlying considerations are usually sensitive and confidential. And even if the Legislature and Governor authorize a lawsuit, the lawsuit could be put on hold for up to a year by just one registered voter, and terminated by 500 voters. Quite simply, the Attorney General's inherent authority to bring litigation cannot and should not be curtailed.
I urge the Committee to vote Ought Not to Pass on LD 1008.
Sincerely,
Aaron M. Frey Attorney General

Testimony in Support of LD 1008: "An Act to Require the Attorney General to Seek Legislative Approval Before Filing Any Civil Suit on Behalf of the State and to Authorize Citizen-initiated Petitions to Move for
Dismissal"
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and the distinguished members of the Committee on Judiciary, my name is Harris Van Pate and I serve as policy analyst for Maine Policy Institute. Maine Policy is a free market think tank, a nonpartisan, non-profit organization that advocates for individual liberty and economic freedom in Maine. Thank you for the opportunity to testify in support of LD 1008.
LD 1008 is a prudent and necessary measure to ensure that Maine's executive branch, particularly the Office of the Attorney General, remains accountable to the people and their elected representatives when pursuing legal actions that could have wide-ranging political, economic, and constitutional implications for the state.
This bill recognizes that when the Attorney General acts in the name of "the State," those actions carry profound consequences--often implicating public policy, the economy, or constitutional principles. It is only fitting that such actions receive legislative authorization, just as the Legislature must approve matters of taxation, appropriations, and regulation. The current unilateral authority of the Attorney General to file civil lawsuits on behalf of the state lacks sufficient democratic oversight.
LD 1008 provides two critical reforms:
- Legislative Oversight of Civil Litigation Initiated by the Attorney General: This bill restores a key check on executive power by requiring legislative approval before the Attorney General may file suit in state or federal court on behalf of the State. In recent years, attorneys general in states nationwide--both Republican and Democrat--have increasingly used litigation to advance partisan agendas or align with national political movements.1 This practice circumvents the legislative process and undermines representative government.
- Citizen-Initiated Petitions for Case Review: LD 1008 also empowers the people of Maine by providing a mechanism for registered voters to initiate a review of any civil case filed by the Attorney General. This democratizes the process and safeguards against politically motivated or unpopular litigation. Temporarily halting proceedings while such a petition is reviewed ensures that citizens have meaningful input before state resources are further expended.
1 "The importance of state attorneys general in shaping federal policy is therefore a fairly recent and important phenomenon." https://scholarship.law.nd.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1728&context=jleg

In Maine, where the Attorney General is entirely unaccountable to the people due to his election via secret ballot, the public must have some oversight of ongoing state lawsuits. Maine's attorney general has recently issued a highly politicized lawsuit against the Trump administration over federal funding distribution. Considering that one of Maine's congressional districts voted for the president, it is logical that the general public should have some sort of input into the decision-making process as to whether to proceed with this lawsuit.2 These reforms are consistent with Maine Policy Institute's longstanding commitment to transparency, limited government, and democratic accountability. No single official, regardless of party, should wield unchecked legal authority to shape public policy through the courts. The state should not advance lawsuits without securing a mandate from the legislative branch, closest to the people and best suited to assess public interest. Finally, this bill does not inhibit the Attorney General from defending the laws or interests of the state as currently permitted. Instead, it introduces a thoughtful framework of accountability when the office seeks to initiate high-stakes litigation that purports to speak on behalf of every Mainer. For these reasons, Maine Policy Institute supports LD 1008 and urges this committee to advance the bill. Thank you for your time and consideration.
2 https://www.wabi.tv/2025/01/29/maine-attorney-general-joins-lawsuit-against-presidents-federal-funding-freeze/

Testifying against

Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on the Judiciary,
my name is Sherma Bellows, I live in Manchester, and I am the Secretary of State. I am testifying
against L.D. 1008.
As a general matter, Maine's Constitutional Officers -- the Attorney General, the State Treasurer and the Secretary of State -- are elected by the members of the Legislature to do the work assigned by the state constitution. These are not clerical positions which require signoff and micromanagement by the
Legislature to conduct our work.
Specific to the Secretary of State's work, L.D. 1008 establishes a new process by which a small group of Mainers could halt the Attorney General's work by petition. The Secretary of State would need to design the petition before it would be circulated and validate the voters upon filing the completed petition with the Department. The number of signatures required (500) and length of time available for
petitioners to collect signatures (one year) is not in line with other citizen-initiated petition processes in
Maine currently, especially since applying for and filing a completed petition require legal action. Other petition processes simply put forward potential changes to rules or laws. For example, potential
changes to laws through the citizen initiative process require voter signatures of at least 10% of the total votes cast in the most recent gubernatorial election (currently 67,682) and petitions may be
circulated for 18 months from issuance.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide this information, and I am happy to answer any questions you may have at the work session.

Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, Distinguished Members of the Judiciary
Committee:
My name is Will Tuell. l represent House District 10 which includes nearly two dozen small communities in central and coastal Washington County, and I am here today to present LD 1008, "An Act to Require the Attorney General to Seek Legislative Approval Before Filing Any Civil Suit on Behalf of the State and to Authorize Citizen-initiated Petitions to Move for Dismissal."
This bill is a companion bill to LD 635, which sought to bar the attorney general from suing Big Oil because it speaks to the bigger question.
Should Maine's Attorney General have the power to enter a civil suit without the
consent of the very people who employ him or her?
If your answer is "Yes, sometimes things come up and we need to be proactive,"
than I would submit this is a proactive piece of legislation that says the Legislature, the employer of Maine's Attorney General, should be able to set
boundaries around what cases the AG may pursue and what cases he or she
may not pursue. It further stipulates that the people who elect us have an
opportunity to demand we bring the AG before us and make him or herjustify his
case before pursuing it.
Whether you or I agree with any given suit -. the "Big Oil" suit was my motivation for this bill - it is problematic that constitutionally elected lawmakers have no input on such endeavors, and should be the standard policy as long as we
appoint our state's top lawyer.
Across the way we are debating whether the people of the State of Maine should
elect the Attorney General. l would argue that until such time as that is passed, their elected representatives should have oversight on what the person occupying that office does or does not pursue in civil court.
Even then, the citizens should have a way to pump the brakes on a suit they find objectionable. That petition process will need some refinement, but I would
encourage the committee to do so so that both legislators and the general public can have confidence that our Attorney General is acting in our best interests.

House District 10

l know this will be seen as inconvenient, hamstringing the AG's office, and will
result in uncomfortable conversations in the Legislature, butjust as our Appropriations Committee oversees the development of our budget, it is
reasonable to expect this committee oversee the AG's civil caseload. lt is also reasonable to suggest that if we have a process to submit bills, present
them to a committee of our peers, and sift them through, so to should our lawyer. l appreciate your time, consideration, and forbearance with me, and look forward to the conversation that this legislation generates. I would also encourage you to
consider LD 635 in tandem with this bill, whenever a work session may be scheduled as it may be that you will favor a more tailored, limited approach rather
than confronting this broader question.
Either way, I thank you for hearing me out.
House District 10
